title: Every word has a tune
hookLine: the Tanakh is chanted with ancient musical notes
carry: where the verse breathes is where its thought divides

cards: Tiny marks, above and below the letters. Open a printed Hebrew Bible and look closely: besides the letters and the vowel dots, there's a third layer of small signs. A little wedge here, a curl there, a dot beside a line.
Those marks are the trope, in Hebrew te'amim, and they tell a reader how to chant. The Torah scroll itself has no vowels and no marks at all, so the reader learns them beforehand.
In the synagogue the Torah is chanted, each word carrying its own short phrase of melody, and the marks say which phrase. This whole library carries its music on the page.

teach.b: The trope does two jobs at once. The first is music: each mark is a little melody, and a verse becomes a chain of them. The second is sense.
The same marks work like punctuation: some say pause here, strongly; some say keep going, these words belong together.

So the tune is also a guide to meaning: where the verse breathes is where its thought divides. Take the first verse of the Torah, in the King James words: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth."

In the Hebrew, the main pause mark falls after God created, and the chant rests there, before the heaven and the earth. The Hebrew word ta'am, the singular of te'amim, can mean taste, and also sense or reason.

And here's a link back to the water gate. When Nehemiah says the Levites read distinctly, gave the sense, and caused the people to understand the reading, the Talmud reads part of that verse as the te'amim themselves.
On that reading, understanding a text and hearing where it divides go together.
Tradition also has more than one melody for the same marks, and some books, like Esther on Purim and Lamentations on the ninth of Av, have tunes of their own.
Lately we've walked through the Writings: wisdom, song, lament, Esther, Daniel, Ezra and Nehemiah, Chronicles. Today, the marks that carry all of it as song.

how: In synagogue, a reader chants the Torah and haftarah portions from the text using the te'amim, and young people preparing for a bar or bat mitzvah learn the trope to chant their portion.

games.q: you're reading Genesis 1:1 aloud in Hebrew, following the trope. where does the main pause fall?
games.why: the main pause mark falls after God created, so the verse rests there before the heaven and the earth.

practice: If you've ever heard Torah chanted, at a synagogue, a bar or bat mitzvah, a recording, let a few notes come back now.
If you haven't, say the first verse of Genesis slowly, pausing after God created, then going on, the heaven and the earth, and let your voice rise and fall a little, any way that feels natural.
